---
title: "A Poisson regression analysis"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The Nettle language rate model asks whether expected reported language density changes with mean growing season. The [discussion of the country counts](poisson-regression.qmd#nettle-country-counts) defines the geopolitical row and explains why country totals may overlap in the languages they include; the Algeria row supplies the numerical units. The [offset page](exposure-offsets.qmd) states the fixed proportional area assumption. We ask four questions: Does a longer mean growing season correspond to a different expected language rate? How uncertain is that association under the row independence approximation? Does the Poisson mean--variance relation fit the observed counts? And which claims remain unavailable because countries and reported languages do not form independent biological sampling units?

The fitted Poisson [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) equals its fitted mean. The printed interval uses a row [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) approximation, even though the discussion of the country counts gives several reasons that neighboring rows may remain related.

```{r}
#| label: load-nettle-application
#| echo: true
nettle <- read.csv("data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv")
correct <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log_area_km2),
               poisson(), nettle)
mismatched <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log10_area_km2),
                  poisson(), nettle)
data.frame(
  offset = c("natural log area", "base-10 log area inserted directly"),
  mgs_coefficient = c(coef(correct)[[2L]], coef(mismatched)[[2L]]),
  rate_ratio = exp(c(coef(correct)[[2L]], coef(mismatched)[[2L]]))
)
```

The primary model is

$$
Y_i\mid\lambda_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),
\qquad
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

Thus $\exp(\widehat\beta_1)$ is the fitted multiplicative change in expected languages per square kilometer for one additional month of mean growing season. A Wald interval on the log-rate scale becomes a rate-ratio interval after exponentiation.

```{r}
#| label: nettle-rate-ratio-uncertainty
#| echo: true
b <- coef(summary(correct))["mean_growing_season_months", ]
link_interval <- b["Estimate"] + qnorm(c(.025, .975)) * b["Std. Error"]
rate_ratio <- exp(b["Estimate"])
rate_ratio_interval <- exp(link_interval)

mgs_example <- range(nettle$mean_growing_season_months)
common_area_km2 <- median(exp(nettle$log_area_km2))
example_counts <- exp(
  log(common_area_km2) + coef(correct)[[1L]] +
    coef(correct)[[2L]] * mgs_example
)
data.frame(estimate = exp(b["Estimate"]), lower = exp(link_interval[1]),
           upper = exp(link_interval[2]))
```

For one additional month of mean growing season, the fitted language rate per
square kilometer is multiplied by `r sprintf("%.3f", rate_ratio)`, with a
row-independent 95% Wald interval from
`r sprintf("%.3f", rate_ratio_interval[[1L]])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", rate_ratio_interval[[2L]])`. At the common illustrative area
of `r format(round(common_area_km2), big.mark = ",")` square kilometers, the two
observed MGS endpoints `r sprintf("%.1f", mgs_example[[1L]])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", mgs_example[[2L]])` months give fitted expected counts of
`r sprintf("%.2f", example_counts[[1L]])` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", example_counts[[2L]])`. Their ratio is determined entirely by
the fitted MGS coefficient and the endpoint difference. It describes the model's
country-row association; countries were not assigned to climates, so the
calculation does not identify a causal climate effect.

The mismatch changes the coefficient because it no longer encodes $\lambda_i=A_i r_i$ with an exposure coefficient of one.

```{r}
#| label: nettle-application-plot
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
nettle$observed_rate <- nettle$language_count / exp(nettle$log_area_km2)
grid <- data.frame(mean_growing_season_months =
  seq(min(nettle$mean_growing_season_months),
      max(nettle$mean_growing_season_months), length.out = 200L))
grid$fitted_rate <- exp(coef(correct)[[1L]] + coef(correct)[[2L]] *
                          grid$mean_growing_season_months)
ggplot(nettle, aes(mean_growing_season_months, observed_rate)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = fitted_rate), color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Mean growing season (months)", y = "Languages per square kilometer") +
  theme_classic()
```

The fitted positive association describes the 74 represented country totals under a
fixed-area-exposure assumption. Country boundaries collect languages, histories,
and documentation practices into one row, while some languages can cross those
boundaries. Countries were not assigned to climates, and the data contain no
intervention that could separate growing season from those other processes.
Nettle's original specification also estimated the area coefficient rather than
fixing it to one.

The Poisson variance restriction should also be checked rather than assumed. Pearson dispersion and the most influential countries diagnose different problems: variance misspecification versus sensitivity to particular design points.

```{r}
#| label: nettle-poisson-checks
#| echo: true
pearson_dispersion <- sum(residuals(correct, type = "pearson")^2) /
  df.residual(correct)
cooks <- cooks.distance(correct)
data.frame(pearson_dispersion,
           most_influential_country = nettle$country[which.max(cooks)],
           maximum_cooks_distance = max(cooks))
```

## Recap and check

1. What happens if base-10 log area is inserted as a natural-log offset? The fixed coefficient no longer represents proportional exposure, and the climate estimate changes.
2. Does a positive fitted rate ratio establish a climate effect? No. It is a descriptive association under the distribution, mean, exposure, and independence assumptions.

The [overdispersion page](count-overdispersion.qmd) interprets the Pearson statistic and routes different failures to different models.
